Overview: The Bayliner 3058 Command Bridge is a compact flybridge cruiser using twin sterndrives and a two-level cabin arrangement to provide more living space than many boats of similar length. The bridge and lower accommodation improve cruising versatility, while machinery access and twin-drive maintenance remain important ownership compromises.

Engine-room working space is limited
Flybridge increases windage and bridge-clearance requirements

Buyers wanting twin-engine handling below 32 feet

ModelCharacter: A compact flybridge cruiser that squeezes dual helms, two sleeping cabins and a convertible dinette into roughly 31 feet. Most surviving examples are sterndrive boats, making it a value-oriented bridge cruiser with more accommodation than machinery access.
DesignLineage: Factory manuals and surviving boats verify the 3058 Command Bridge in the early 1990s.
The 3058 combines Bayliner's hardtop/express interior packaging with an upper command bridge.
It is distinct from the 3055 Sunbridge despite similar length and shared era.
Exact full production chronology is poorly documented; B-Atlas uses the directly verified 1991–92 window rather than inventing a broader span.
OwnershipCharacter: Twin sterndrive examples offer performance and redundancy but can be labor-intensive in older freshwater/saltwater service. Bridge enclosure, drive condition, engine access and transom/core moisture deserve close survey attention.

ModelCharacter: A compact Europa-style trawler that adds extended flybridge overhangs and sheltered side/aft decks to the traditional Island Gypsy 32 formula. It combines unusually good weather protection and a warm teak interior in a genuinely small cruising footprint.
DesignLineage: Documented as a distinct 32 Europa production model from 1989 into the early 2000s.
It shares the 32-foot Island Gypsy family dimensions and single-stateroom sedan mission but adds characteristic Europa overhangs.
Halvorsen history records late examples, including 2005–2006 32 Eurosedans built in southern China.
Later single-Cummins boats provide more power while preserving the displacement-speed cruising character.
OwnershipCharacter: Very attractive for a cruising couple wanting covered decks and modest size. Exterior teak and aging deck/window details create maintenance exposure, but the single-engine drivetrain remains straightforward and economical.

Strengths: Traditional teak interior and practical cruising layout
Protected shaft-drive running gear and economical low-to-moderate-speed operation

CommonProblems: Fuel tank side-seam scaling from window track leaks, deck core softening under teak overlays.
TypicalMission: Long-range family coastal loop transits and traditional liveaboard residency.
AvoidIf: You need modern systems with minimal refit exposure

ModelCharacter: The classic aft-cabin Island Gypsy: a heavily built, two-stateroom trawler with teak-rich interior, full walkaround decks and a full-length prop-protecting keel. It offers true extended-cruising accommodation without moving into 40-foot yacht scale.
DesignLineage: Powerboat Guide documents the 36 Classic from 1978–2001 and treats the 36 Quad Cabin as the same core model family.
Several two-stateroom floorplans were offered over the production run, with varying berth and galley arrangements.
The 36 Europa is a distinct sedan/covered-cockpit configuration with different deckhouse architecture.
Island Gypsy's later sub-40-foot range evolved beyond the original 36, with a 39-foot successor appearing around 1999.
OwnershipCharacter: Comfortable for a couple with guests and still conventional mechanically, but teak decks/rails, multiple tanks and decades of system modifications create substantial survey and refit exposure. Individual boats can vary greatly because factory layouts and later owner changes were numerous.
